contraindications: Fosphenytoin and phenytoin: ineffective for INH-induced SE (wrong mechanism); do not use.
Succinylcholine: contraindicated if pseudocholinesterase inhibition is also suspected; use rocuronium.
interactions: Isoniazid + benzodiazepines: benzodiazepines require synaptic GABA to work; INH irreversibly inactivates pyridoxal-5-phosphate (PLP) — the cofactor for GABA synthesis — causing GABA depletion; explains complete benzodiazepine resistance in INH-induced SE.
Fosphenytoin/phenytoin + INH SE: fosphenytoin targets voltage-gated sodium channels — INH SE is GABA-depletion mediated, not sodium channel mediated; fosphenytoin is ineffective; do not use.
output.proposed: isoniazid (INH) 10-15 g accidental ingestion + IV pyridoxine 5 g antidote
warnings: Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) 5 g IV is the specific antidote: 1 g pyridoxine per gram of INH ingested; give 5 g empirically if amount unknown; administer over 30-60 minutes; seizures typically stop within 20-60 minutes.
After pyridoxine restores GABA synthesis, benzodiazepines become effective as adjunctive agents.

results.key_finding: INH SE is benzodiazepine-resistant because INH depletes pyridoxal-5-phosphate, preventing GABA synthesis. Pyridoxine is the specific antidote: 1g IV per gram of INH ingested; if amount unknown, give 5g IV empirically. Fosphenytoin is ineffective. After pyridoxine, benzodiazepines become effective once GABA is restored. Prognosis excellent with early pyridoxine administration.

metadata.clinical_pearl: Benzodiazepine-resistant SE in young healthy patient = toxic antidote SE. INH depletes GABA → pyridoxine 5g IV is the antidote. Standard UDS misses INH. Fosphenytoin will fail. Pyridoxine works in 20-45 minutes.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: 7 required + 1 optional; INH-induced refractory SE — pyridoxine is the specific antidote; teaching is recognizing B6-deficient SE and the futility of AED escalation without antidote; 2 grounded red herrings.
metadata.pitfalls: Using fosphenytoin/phenytoin for INH SE; escalating benzodiazepines without antidote; not considering toxic etiology for benzodiazepine-resistant SE in healthy patient
metadata.revision_reason: per-case audit: 2 assay(s) the gold standard requires were never delivered, so an agent doing what the gold says saw nothing; reported as exclusions, which is what the case asserts by asserting its diagnosis
metadata.teaching_points: INH toxicity mechanism (PLP depletion → GABA depletion → benzodiazepine resistance); pyridoxine as antidote; fosphenytoin ineffective; standard UDS misses INH; benzodiazepine refractoriness = toxic etiology clue

patient.history_present_illness: A 31-year-old White female pharmacy technician was brought to the emergency department after her roommate found her convulsing. EMS reports she was in generalized status epilepticus — continuous tonic-clonic activity for at least 8 minutes before EMS arrived, continuing on arrival. She was given IV lorazepam 4 mg with no response. Another 4 mg lorazepam was given with no response. She was intubated in the field and given IV fosphenytoin 20 mg/kg PE with continued seizure activity (unresponsive). She has no prior history of epilepsy. She has no known medical conditions. Her roommate found no medications in the apartment initially. She is currently on levetiracetam drip started by ED as third-line agent. Seizures have not fully stopped — intermittent clinical movements persist. Critical history discovered AFTER admission (45 minutes in): a colleague at the pharmacy calls and reports the patient had accidentally ingested a large amount of isoniazid (INH) — she was preparing a multi-dose vial and accidentally consumed the powder (approximately 10-15 grams) after a chemical spill incident at work earlier today. The colleague only just learned what had happened.
